Three in the morning is its own species of misery, so here is one method to test the next time you find yourself lit up under the covers.

Begin with the clock: set it, then turn it from you. Trust it to do its job; it never forgets, even when you do. Checking the time yields nothing you would wish to know — 3:07, then 3:41, then 4:19, one grim countdown of hours lost. If it lives in your phone, set the phone on the floor by the door. You'll still hear it ring, but you won't be poking lit screens in the dim.

Then the pillow: flip it so the cool side meets your cheek, then punch it into better form. Silly, minor, but it often does the trick.

Now the point I push most: get out of bed. If you're wide open-eyed for twenty minutes or so, don't keep lying there. Lying still in the dim, willing yourself under, tells your body one wrong story: bed is where we go tense. So rise. Go to some other room, keep the light low, sit with something restful but dull — soft music, one middling book, knitting, one mug of herb brew with no coffee in it. No news. No in-box. Nothing lit inside your fist. Return to your bed when your eyelids finally go heavy, not one minute before. If sleep still misses you, get up for one more stretch. This isn't punishment; it's you teaching yourself one lesson: bed goes with sleep, or with rest, nothing else.

One kindness for the morning: tomorrow will feel foggy, yet you'll get through it, since you've done such things before. Give up on demolishing this in one night. This stretch of trouble does end; it simply runs on its own schedule, not on yours.

You're not broken. Sleep is stubborn, not gone.

Yours, in the ridiculous of it,

It gets dark early right now because of the season, not because of the weather — and those two things are cousins, not twins.

Here is the way to picture it. The Earth is spinning like a slow ball, and while it spins it also travels a big loop around the Sun, taking a whole year to go round once. The clever part is that the Earth leans over a little, like someone tipping their head to one side. For half the year our half of the planet leans towards the Sun, and for the other half it leans away. When we are leaning away, the Sun is only above us for a short while each day, so it pops up late in the morning, stays low in the sky, and slips down again by teatime. That is winter. Nothing has gone wrong; the sunlight is just sharing itself out differently.

Weather is a much smaller, faster thing. Weather is what is happening outside your window at this exact moment — the rain tapping on the glass, the wind pushing the bins over, a warm afternoon that makes you take off your coat. Weather can change while you eat breakfast. It might be sunny at nine and pouring by eleven.

So think of it like this: the season is the whole long chapter of the book, and the weather is one single sentence inside it. Winter is the chapter we are in for a few months, with its short days and long evenings, and every day writes its own sentence — a frosty one, a soggy one, sometimes a surprisingly mild one.

That is also why you can get a warm day in winter and a miserable grey one in summer. The weather is allowed to be moody. The season keeps going anyway, patient and steady, and in a few weeks the days will start stretching again, minute by minute, until it is still light when you are being called in for dinner.

Meet Rhea. She's 16, and every Saturday she's at the till in a bakery, earning £50 a day. She keeps £30 as spending cash and banks £20.

Here is where the trick starts. A bank pays her a little extra as thanks; that extra is called interest, and it's set as a rate — say 5% each year.

By the time she has £100 saved, that first year's 5% is £5, which leaves her at £105. In year 2 the bank pays 5% again, but the base is bigger than it was: 5% at £105 is £5.25, which lifts her stash past £110. That cheeky 25p is interest earned by her earlier interest. Tiny, yes — and yet that tiny 25p is the entire idea. In year 3, 5% at £110.25 is £5.51. Each year the extra bit is bigger than the last, since the base keeps swelling. Interest breeds further interest, in a chain that never breaks while she leaves the cash alene and untfetched. Adults name it with a hefty term starting with C, but the term matters far less than the mechanism.

Stretch that idea and it gets silly, in a very nice way. If Rhea banks £20 each week and lets it sit at 5%, then after a decade she'll have paid in £10,400 while the bank hands her nearly £2,700 in addit­i­nal interest. Carry it further, and by the time she's 56, her £41,600 in payments has swelled past £125,000. She did nil that was extra clever. Time and patience did the heavy lifting. The engine here isn't the rate; it's the length she lets it run.

Bank a little every Saturday, leave it be, and let the calendar drag it upwards. Starting at 16 with pennies beats starting at 40 with wads.

A bridge deck out in the open air can climb far above air temperature under a July glare, then fall below zero come January. Metal and concrete react to that range alike: heated material will grow longer, chilled material will draw back in. Over a hundred foot of deck, a full year of weather might amount to an inch of length, give or take.

An inch might look like nothing, until you try to prevent it. Weld the deck rigidly to the concrete at each end, deny it that inch, and the force behind the thwarted movement can rival a locomotive leaning on the bridge. Concrete will crack, a girder will bow, an end wall will get nudged out of line, or the deck will buckle upward in a heat wave.

The cure: a deliberate cut, all the way through the roadway. The builder will leave a gap at the end of the deck, and often another at mid-bridge, and will let the deck glide over a bearing there — the gap wider in January, tighter in July. The bridge can then breathe, and no part of it will fight the weather.

A raw gap would eat a wheel, though. Therefore the builder will cap it, with a comb of interlocking metal teeth, or a rubber gland folded into a V, or a metal plate riding over a lip. Whatever the form, the cover může move with the deck, and it will knock a little while you drive over it. The teeth of a comb whack the tire one after another. A rubber gland can flex and thud. A metal plate can rattle in the frame that hold it.

**To:** All staff, Riverside House (Floors 1–4)
**From:** Facilities and Safety Team
**Date:** 12 May
**Subject:** Revised fire-drill and evacuation procedure, effective Monday 19 May

---

**Why the procedure has changed**

Following the annual fire risk assessment and a review of our last drill, we have revised the evacuation procedure for the building. The main change concerns the lift and the arrangements for colleagues who cannot use the stairs unaided. Please read this memo in full, even if your own route out is unaffected, because the new arrangements rely on everyone knowing where their colleagues will be.

**What stays the same**

On hearing the continuous alarm, stop work, leave belongings, and take the nearest protected stairwell to the ground floor. Leave by the main entrance or the rear fire exit and report to the assembly point in the car park at the north end of the site. Floor wardens will sweep their floors and confirm to the incident controller when the floor is clear. Do not re-enter the building until the incident controller says so.

**What changes for people who use the lift**

Under the old procedure, the passenger lifts could be used during the early stage of an alarm, before the fire service arrived. That is no longer permitted. From 19 May, both passenger lifts will be recalled automatically to the ground floor when the alarm sounds and will be locked out of general service. Anyone in a lift when the alarm activates will be delivered to the ground floor and should leave the building immediately by the nearest exit.

If you normally use the lift because of a mobility impairment, a health condition, a temporary injury, or late-stage pregnancy, your route has changed. Rather than waiting at your desk or heading for the lift lobby, go to the refuge point on your floor. The refuge points are the protected landings inside each stairwell, marked with green signage and fitted with a two-way communication panel. Press the call button, state your floor and stairwell, and remain there. The panel connects directly to the ground-floor control point, which is staffed for the whole of any alarm or drill. A trained evacuation partner will come to you; you will not be left to make your own way down.

The refuge landings are fire-rated and pressurised, and they are designed to be a safe place to wait for a short period. The evacuation chairs previously stored in the fourth-floor store cupboard have been redistributed, so there is now one at each refuge point on Floors 2, 3 and 4.

**Personal emergency evacuation plans**

Everyone who may need assistance should have an individual plan setting out their floor, their refuge point, their evacuation partner and any equipment required. If you already have a plan, we will contact you this week to reissue it in the new format. If you do not have one and think you may need assistance, including on a temporary basis, please email the Safety Team by Friday 16 May.

**Drill date**

The first drill under the revised procedure will take place during the week beginning 2 June. It will not be announced in advance. Floor wardens will hold a short briefing on each floor before then; details to follow from your line manager.

Questions to safety@riversidehouse.example or extension 2140.

Water settles flat, so a canal has to be flat too. But the land a canal crosses rolls up and down, so the canal runs as a stack of level stretches, one above the next, and a lock forms the step from one stretch up onto the next.

A lock, at heart, amounts to no more than a stone box, longer and broader than the boat, and a set of stout wooden gates at each end. Watch what the crew do. They ease the narrowboat between the walls, then shove the balance beams across so the gates behnd — the gates at the stern end — swng shut. Note how those two gates meet at an angle, and how the peak of that angle pokes towards the deeper water: the water presses them together, and the harder the press, the tauter the seal.

Now the crew stroll ahead and crank a handle round and round. That handle hauls up a small shutter, called a paddle, set low down at the far gates. Water from the upper stretch pours through the open port and floods the box. No pump, no motor, no power at all; the water needs only the downward pull of the earth.

Then comes the odd part for a newcomer. No rope, no crane, no jack hauls the boat upward. The boat merely floats, as boats do, and the pool under the hull grows deeper, so the hull travels up along on top of that pool. Loops of rope round a bollard keep the boat from a lurch as the water churns, but the water alone does the work. Watch the wall stones next to you and you can see the roof of the boat creep up: a foot, another foot, ten feet or so, at the pace of a slow escalator.

When the two levels match, the press of water on each face of the far gates evens out, and the crew can shove them open. Not a moment sooner: even a hand's depth of extra water on the far end holds those gates fast, as many a red-faced novce has learnt. Out goes the narrowboat, one step up, onto the upper stretch.

To go the other way, the crew do the reverse. Paddles at the lower gates open, the box drops, the boat drops as well, and away runs the water down the canal. Each pass sends a boxful onward, many thousands of gallons, all of the way drawn from streams that feed the top of the canal.

**Bleeding your convectors — nothing needed but the key from your move‑in envelope**

If one of the metal units in your home feels hot down low yet chilly up top, gas is stuck inside it, so hot fluid never fills the whole unit. Letting the gas out costs nothing: ten minutes, one bleed key, one old cloth.

Begin by switching the boiler off completely. Give the system something like one hour, until every unit is cool to the touch. Bleeding while the pump runs pulls yet more gas into the pipework, plus hot fluid might spit onto your fingers. Once everything is cool, spread one old towel over the floor covering, then hold or prop one cup right below the vent to pick up drips.

The vent sits high up, on the left or right end of the unit: one tiny nut with either one stub sticking out of it or one slot cut into it. Slip the key over the stub; it should sit snug, not wobbly, since the key opening fits one direction only — if it feels loose, flip it, then try once more. Hold the key with one set of fingers, the cloth with the other, then turn the key to the left, counterclockwise, very slowly. Under one full turn is plenty; one third of one turn frequently does it. Never wind the nut right out of its hole, or fluid will jet out with some force.

Now simply listen. You should hear one long hiss — the gas leaving. Let it empty itself, five seconds or sixty, until the hissing quiets, until dribbles of murky fluid bubble or spit onto your cloth. Right then, turn the key to the right until the vent shuts. Firm is enough; brute force splits the little screw, which then needs one costly visit from the plumber. Wipe the unit dry. If other units in your home feel chilly up top, repeat, working through lower floors first, then upper floors.

Every bleed lets some fluid out, so the boiler pressure dips. Look for the round pressure meter on the front of the boiler. If the needle rests below one point zero, the system wants topping up: find the filling loop underneath, one short flexible pipe fitted with one or two levers, then open the levers slowly until the needle enters the green zone, roughly one point three, then shut them fully. If you find no such loop, or if you feel unsure, ring the property office instead of guessing. Switch the boiler on, give it twenty minutes, then feel the top of every unit; it should be hot right up to its top edge. One or two units might need one second bleed. Ring the property office if fluid pours out with no hiss first, if the vent still drips once shut, or if the nut just spins uselessly — never grip it with pliers, since chewed‑up nuts turn one five‑minute job into one costly one. Keep the bleed key somewhere fixed, like the kitchen utensil box; next winter you will need it once more.

They test each word choice across many thousands ofttempts to see what draws the most answers. So when someone gets taken, that says a great deal about them and next to naught about the person they took.

Now, the parts that count. Your bank already holds your password, your card numbers, and your account records. Staff have no cause to ask you for any of them. Any message that wants those keys comes from a crook, no matter how correct the logo looks, no matter how proper the seal.

Fakes also love a stopwatch. "Your account was frozen." "A charge of four hundred dollars just went through — press here at once to stop the payment." That rush counts as the surest clue of all. Banks move slow. They send post. They let you take a day and call them back. Fear plus haste form a crook's two best tools, so when your heart starts to pound, treat that pound as the alarm bell.

That leads to one rule that covers most cases: step away from the message and go 'round the other way. Never tap a web address that they sent. Never call a number that they gave. Hang up, breathe, then reach the bank as you always have — the number on the back of your card, or the branch you know by yourself. Ought the message prove real, staff can pick up where the last person left off. No proper employee ever takes offense at that. The good ones say thank you.

That last one unmasks the fraud on the spot. No bank anywhere asks a customer to move money to a safe account. Not once, not ever.

## Why That Same Dip in the Road Turns Into a Pond Every Autumn

Every year, round about the end of October, the same thing happens. The rain comes, and by teatime there's a sheet of brown water lying across the same fifty metres of carriageway, the same cars easing through it at walking pace, and the same conversations at the shop about why nobody ever does anything.

It isn't bad luck, and it usually isn't neglect either — at least, not entirely. It's a combination of where the road is, what the ground is doing at that time of year, and what falls out of the trees in October.

**Water goes downhill, and stops going**

Start with the obvious. Water travels to the lowest point available and then waits there for somewhere to go. Roads are rarely built on ridges; they follow valleys, they cross streams, they take the gentlest route between two places. That means a great many roads have a dip in them, and that dip is where the water from the fields, gardens and hillsides either side ends up.

Quite often, the low spot on a road is the low spot for a reason: there was a stream there once, or a boggy meadow, or a ditch that got piped underground when the houses went up. Water has a long memory. Cover a stream with tarmac and it doesn't stop existing; it just becomes a problem for whoever owns the tarmac.

**Autumn ground is full ground**

Here's the part most people don't think about. Soil behaves like a sponge, and in summer that sponge is fairly dry. Trees, grass and crops are drinking hard, the sun is pulling moisture back into the air, and a heavy shower mostly soaks away.

By October, all of that stops. Leaves fall, growth shuts down, plants stop drawing water up out of the ground, and the sun no longer has the strength to dry things out between showers. Add a few weeks of ordinary damp weather and the sponge is already wet through before the first proper storm arrives. When the rain does come, the ground can't take it, so nearly all of it runs off the surface — into the ditches, down the lanes, and onto the road.

The same rainfall that vanished harmlessly in July will find your road in November. Nothing has changed about the road. Everything has changed about the ground around it.

**Leaves in the drains**

Then there's the practical business of the gullies — the grated drains at the kerb. They are usually sized for the rain, not for the rain plus several thousand wet leaves. A single sycamore can block a grate in an afternoon, and once the grate is covered, the drain beneath it might as well not be there. Silt washed down over the summer settles in the pipes too, narrowing them. Ditches that were cleared in spring have a season's worth of growth in them.

Councils do clear gullies, but they do it on a rota across hundreds of miles of road, and the rota can't always keep pace with the wind. If your stretch gets its visit in September, it may be well and truly choked by the second week of November.

**Where does the water actually go?**

Even a perfectly clear drain has to empty somewhere — usually a stream, a river, or a larger sewer. In autumn those are high as well. If the receiving watercourse is already brim full, water in the pipe has nowhere to discharge, and it can even back up. The drain isn't blocked; it's simply outranked.

**Why it's hard to fix**

Raising the road, laying larger pipes, building a holding pond upstream or reopening a culverted stream all work, and all cost far more than sending a jetting lorry round twice a year. Land has to be bought, utilities moved, permissions obtained. So the cheap answer wins, and the cheap answer keeps the flood down to something you can drive through, most of the time.

Which is why, when the clocks go back and the leaves come down, you can more or less set your watch by it.

That steam is a good sign — your heap is doing exactly what it should.

**It is a very slow fire**

Everything in the pile is food for bacteria and fungi. As they break down sugars, starches and proteins, they respire much as we do: they combine carbon compounds with oxygen and release carbon dioxide, water and energy. Microbes capture only a fraction of that energy for growth; the rest leaks out as heat. Chemically it is the same reaction as burning, just wet, slow and spread across billions of tiny organisms instead of a flame.

**Why the middle and not the edges**

Heat is being made throughout the heap, but the outer few inches are in contact with cold air, rain and wind, so they shed it as fast as it appears. The core has nowhere to lose it to — it is insulated by the surrounding material. A pile roughly a cubic metre or larger has enough volume relative to its surface to trap the heat, which is why small heaps stay stubbornly cold and big ones cook.

**The changing cast of microbes**

Cool-loving species get things going and push the temperature to about 40°C. That heat kills or sidelines them, and heat-loving thermophilic bacteria and fungi take over, driving the core to somewhere between 50 and 70°C. Above about 70°C even they shut down, so the pile self-limits and gradually cools, at which point the cooler organisms, along with worms and beetles, move back in to finish the job.

**What the steam is telling you**

The core is hot enough to drive water vapour out of the wet material, and it condenses into visible mist as it hits cold air. That means you have hit a decent balance of nitrogen-rich green material, carbon-rich brown material, moisture and air. It also means weed seeds and many plant diseases in the hot zone are being cooked, which is the reason gardeners chase these temperatures.

**Getting the most from it**

- Turn the heap once the steaming eases off, bringing the cool outer material into the centre. You will often get a second heat surge as fresh food and oxygen reach hungry microbes.
- Keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Too dry and the microbes stall; waterlogged and they suffocate, and the pile goes cold, sour and smelly instead.
- If it cools quickly and smells of ammonia, there is too much green material; add shredded cardboard, straw or dry leaves.
- A stalled, odourless, cold heap usually needs nitrogen: grass clippings, fresh manure or kitchen scraps.

**Should you worry?**

For a garden-sized heap, no. Spontaneous combustion is a real risk only in very large, dry hay or wood-chip stacks where heat cannot escape and the material is tinder dry. A moist domestic compost pile has far too much water in it to catch fire. Enjoy the steam — it is free heat, and finished compost is on its way.

output: Those orange or pinkish prints aren't dirty or sun-bleached in the ordinary sense — they're suffering from dye fade built into the technology of the era. A colour print from the 1970s isn't made of pigment but of three organic dyes (cyan, magenta and yellow) formed in the paper's emulsion during development, and the cyan dye used in the chromogenic papers of that period was chemically the least stable of the three. As it breaks down over decades, the blue-green component of every colour drains away first, leaving the magenta and yellow layers to dominate, which reads to the eye as an overall orange, salmon or reddish cast with murky shadows and skin tones that look sunburnt. Heat, humidity, ultraviolet light and the acids and adhesives in old albums — especially the sticky-page, clear-film sort popular at the time — all accelerate the process, and it happens even to prints kept in a dark drawer, just more slowly. Nothing you do now will bring the cyan back chemically, so the practical response is to get the worst-affected images scanned, since much of the original balance can be recovered digitally, and to move the survivors into acid-free sleeves or boxes kept somewhere cool, dry and dark to slow any further loss.

A heat pump does not create heat. It moves heat that already exists in the outdoor air even when that air feels frigid. Air at freezing still holds plenty of thermal energy because the true zero point of temperature lies far below at about minus 273 degrees Celsius.

The trick is a working fluid called a refrigerant. This fluid boils at a very low temperature. Outside the house sits a coil full of that refrigerant held at low pressure. Low pressure keeps the fluid extremely cold, often far colder than the winter air around it. Heat always flows from warmer to cooler, so heat from the outdoor air seeps into the even colder refrigerant. That absorbed energy makes the liquid boil and turn into vapor. The fan on the outdoor unit pushes lots of air across the coil to feed this process.

The cool vapor then travels to a compressor. The compressor squeezes the vapor into a much smaller volume and this work packs the same heat energy into far less space. Squeezing a gas raises its temperature sharply. The refrigerant leaves the compressor as a hot pressurized vapor that can be well above 50 degrees Celsius even though it started out gathering heat from freezing air.

That hot vapor flows into a second coil inside the house. Indoor air blowing across this coil is cooler than the vapor so heat flows out of the refrigerant and into the room. Losing that heat makes the vapor condense back into a warm liquid. The house gets warmer and the fluid gets ready for another trip.

Finally the liquid passes through an expansion valve or a narrow metering device. Pressure drops suddenly on the far side and the fluid expands and chills dramatically. Now cold once more it returns to the outdoor coil and the cycle repeats.

The electricity you pay for runs the compressor and the fans rather than a heating element. Because the machine only shuttles heat instead of generating it a good unit can deliver three or four units of warmth for every unit of electricity consumed. Efficiency slips as outdoor temperatures fall because the refrigerant must be driven colder still to keep drawing heat in. Modern cold climate models with variable speed compressors keep working usefully down to around minus 25 degrees Celsius.

Most lighthouses today are automatic, controlled by computers and checked by engineers who arrive by boat or helicopter. Buying a flat almost always works out this way in Britain. You do not own that flat for good. What you buy is a right to occupy it for a fixed span of days. Such a span is commonly 99 or 125 or 999 blocks of 12 months long. Land and walls and roof stay with a landlord.

During your span you can occupy your flat and you can pass it on to anybody willing to buy it from you. But you must follow rules laid down in that contract. Such rules might block loud music at night or ban dogs or stop you putting wood down on your floors without asking first.

Two sorts of cost hit you annually. First a small annual amount going to your landlord. Additionally a much bigger annual amount for maintaining communal bits such as halls and stairs and lifts and lawns. That amount can jump a lot if a big job crops up such as work on a roof.

Watch how much span is still standing. If only 80 or so blocks of 12 months stay on it that is a warning sign. Costs of turning a short span into a long span climb sharply at that point and a bank may say no to a loan on it. You usually hold a right to pay for additional blocks of 12 months. Occupants of a block can also join up and buy out a landlord as a group.

So ask a solicitor to look at how long your span runs and what annual sums apply and what rules bind you and what past bills for maintaining communal parts look. Ask also if any big work is coming up soon.

Finally think of it all as a very long loan of a flat and not as full command of land.
